content: Staphylococcus bacteria are capable of causing a wide range of infections in humans and animals. These infections can occur either through the production of toxins or by direct invasion of tissues. Staphylococcal toxins are a frequent cause of food poisoning, as the bacteria can proliferate in improperly stored food. One particularly pathogenic species, Staphylococcus aureus, is known to infect wounds. These bacteria are resilient and can survive on dry surfaces, which increases the likelihood of transmission. Staphylococcus aureus is also associated with toxic shock syndrome. During the 1980s, certain tampons facilitated the rapid growth of S. aureus, which released toxins that were absorbed into the bloodstream, leading to severe systemic effects. Additionally, any infection caused by S. aureus can result in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, a condition characterized by a cutaneous reaction to exotoxins absorbed into the bloodstream. This bacterium can also cause a form of septicemia known as pyaemia, which can be life-threatening. A significant concern is the emergence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), which has become a major cause of hospital-acquired infections. MRSA is also increasingly recognized as a cause of community-acquired infections. Another species, Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, is a coagulase-positive staphylococcus that resides on the skin of domestic dogs and cats. While it can occasionally infect humans as a zoonosis, this is rare. This organism can also carry genetic material that confers resistance to multiple antibiotics. Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative species, is a commensal organism found on human skin. However, it can cause severe infections in immunocompromised individuals and in patients with central venous catheters. Staphylococcus saprophyticus, another coagulase-negative species, is part of the normal vaginal flora. It is predominantly implicated in genitourinary tract infections, particularly in sexually active young women. In recent years, other Staphylococcus species, such as S. lugdunensis, S. schleiferi, and S. caprae, have been identified as causes of human infections. Lastly, Staphylococcus aureus is one of the most common pathogens responsible for closed-space infections of the fingertips, a condition known as paronychia.
